questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct ε–N definition of $a_n \to L$ as $n \to \infty$?

options.text: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n > N$, $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$.
options.explanation: This is the standard definition. Note the quantifier order: ε is chosen first (by the challenger), then N is produced in response, then the condition holds for all subsequent n.

options.text: There exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and all $n > N$, $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$.
options.explanation: Swapping the quantifiers makes this a much stronger and usually false statement: a single N would have to work for all ε simultaneously, including arbitrarily small ones.
This is circular: it defines a limit using another limit. The ε–N definition is what makes 'tends to zero' itself precise.
Missing the quantifier over ε and the N condition entirely — this would require the sequence to be within ε of L from the very start, for all ε.

options.text: Every bounded sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ has a convergent subsequence.
options.explanation: Correct. The theorem uses the completeness of ℝ (specifically the supremum axiom). It fails in ℚ, where a bounded sequence of rationals may converge to an irrational.
That is the completeness of ℝ (or the Cauchy completeness theorem) — a related but distinct result.
That is the Monotone Convergence Theorem, also a consequence of completeness but a different statement.

options.text: Every continuous function on a closed interval attains its maximum.
options.explanation: That is the Extreme Value Theorem. Bolzano-Weierstrass is used in its proof, but the statements are different.

questions.stem: Why does the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}$ (the harmonic series) diverge, despite $\frac{1}{n} \to 0$?

options.text: The terms $\frac{1}{n}$ do not decrease fast enough: grouping gives $\frac{1}{2} + (\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}) + (\frac{1}{5}+\cdots+\frac{1}{8}) + \cdots$, each group exceeding $\frac{1}{2}$.
options.explanation: This is Oresme's classic grouping argument (c.1350), rediscovered many times. Each bracketed group is greater than 1/2, so partial sums grow without bound.
No convergent series has terms that are eventually zero (unless all terms are zero). The condition $a_n \to 0$ is necessary but not sufficient for convergence.

options.text: Because the ratio test gives limit 1, which implies divergence.
options.explanation: When the ratio test gives limit exactly 1, it is inconclusive — it neither confirms convergence nor divergence. The ratio test fails here.

options.text: Because it is an alternating series.
options.explanation: The harmonic series $\sum 1/n$ is not alternating — all terms are positive.

questions.stem: Which property of $\mathbb{R}$ distinguishes it from $\mathbb{Q}$ and makes analysis work?

options.text: Completeness: every non-empty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound.
options.explanation: The supremum axiom (or completeness axiom) is what makes ℝ 'gapless'. It is not a theorem — it is part of the definition of the real numbers, capturing the intuition that ℝ has no 'holes'.

options.text: Countability: the real numbers are countably infinite.
options.explanation: The real numbers are uncountably infinite — one of Cantor's great discoveries. The rationals are countably infinite.

options.text: Archimedean property: for any $x \in \mathbb{R}$ there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n > x$.
options.explanation: The Archimedean property holds for ℝ (and for ℚ), but it does not distinguish ℝ from ℚ — both are Archimedean.

options.text: Density: between any two real numbers there is another real number.
options.explanation: Density holds in ℚ as well — between any two rationals lies another rational. It does not distinguish ℝ from ℚ.
